title: Decimals and place value: moving the point, leading zeros and tenfold errors
blurb: Read every digit's true value, move the decimal point the right number of places, and write doses so they cannot be misread tenfold.
question: A prescription chart shows a dose written as ".5 mg". A colleague reads it as 5 mg. How large is the error, and how should the dose have been written?

teach.body: Place value means a digit's worth depends on where it sits relative to the decimal point. In 2.75 mg, the 2 is units, the 7 is tenths (0.7) and the 5 is hundredths (0.05). Plain English: the decimal point is the anchor, and each step left of it is ten times bigger, each step right ten times smaller. Almost every Part A error that matters clinically is a decimal point in the wrong place.

teach.caption: Row 2 is 2.75; row 3 is 0.125. Read across: 0.125 = 1 tenth + 2 hundredths + 5 thousandths.
Count the zeros in the multiplier: that is how many places the point moves.

teach.body: Write a zero before a decimal point when the value is below 1: 0.5 mg, never .5 mg, because the point can be missed and the dose read as 5 mg. Never add a trailing zero after a whole number: 5 mg, not 5.0 mg, which can be read as 50 mg. Pearson's answer rules match this: ".9 mL" was marked wrong on the practice test, and Pearson tells candidates not to add extra zeros (enter 1.5, not 1.50).

teach.caption: Each place the point moves multiplies or divides the dose by ten.

teach.h: Worked example: Ward 4, a morning drug round
items: Staff nurse Amara Okafor sees "0.25 mg" prescribed. A solution contains 0.05 mg in each 1 mL.
Estimate first: 0.25 is five times 0.05, so about 5 mL.
Calculate: 0.25 ÷ 0.05 = 25 ÷ 5 (move both points two places right) = 5 mL.
Sense check: had she misread 0.25 as 2.5, she would have drawn up 50 mL: ten times too much, and an implausible oral volume.
She types 5 mL: no trailing zero, correct unit.

teach.text: The classic tenfold error is the missing leading zero (.5 read as 5) or the added trailing zero (5.0 read as 50). When dividing by a decimal, move the point in BOTH numbers by the same number of places before you divide.

items: Each column left of the point is ten times bigger; each column right is ten times smaller.
x10, x100, x1000 moves the point right 1, 2, 3 places; ÷ moves it left.
Always a leading zero (0.5); never a trailing zero (5, not 5.0).
Estimate before you calculate so a tenfold slip stands out.
Number-only answer boxes take digits and one point: no commas, no unit.

summary: You can now read the value of every digit in a dose, move the decimal point correctly when multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 or 1000, and write answers with a leading zero and no trailing zeros. You can also spot a tenfold error before it reaches the person.

A.q: A solution contains 0.3 mg in each 1 mL. How many milligrams are in 10 mL?
A.why: 0.3 mg x 10 = 3 mg: multiplying by 10 moves the point one place right. Sense check: 10 mL must hold ten times what 1 mL holds.

whyNot.1: Divided by 10 instead of multiplying: 10 mL holds more than 1 mL, not less.
whyNot.2: Moved the point two places; multiplying by 10 moves it one place.
whyNot.3: This is the amount in 1 mL; it has not been multiplied by 10.

A.q: A total of 4.5 mg is divided equally into 10 doses. How many milligrams are in each dose? Write your answer to two decimal places.
A.why: 4.5 ÷ 10 = 0.45 mg: dividing by 10 moves the point one place left, and the leading zero is written. Sense check: ten doses of about half a milligram make 4.5 mg.

whyNot.0: This is the total; it has not been divided by 10.
whyNot.1: Moved the point two places; dividing by 10 moves it one place left.
whyNot.3: Multiplied by 10 instead of dividing: each dose must be smaller than the total.

A.q: Which way of writing half a milligram meets safe prescribing practice and the Pearson answer format?
A.why: 0.5 mg has the leading zero that stops a tenfold misreading and no extra trailing zero.

whyNot.0: Without a leading zero the point can be missed and the dose read as 5 mg; Pearson marked ".9 mL" wrong.
whyNot.1: The trailing zero adds nothing and is not the accepted Pearson form.
whyNot.3: Fractions are not used for doses on charts or in Part A answer boxes.

B.q: A dose of 0.25 mg was prescribed but 2.5 mg was given. How many times the prescribed dose was given? Write your answer as a whole number.
B.why: 2.5 ÷ 0.25 = 10. The point moved one place, so the dose was ten times too large.

whyNot.1: 2.5 is one place, not two, away from 0.25.
whyNot.2: This is the difference in milligrams, not how many times larger the dose was.
whyNot.3: A factor of 1000 would be a three-place slip, such as mg read as micrograms.

B.q: A person is prescribed 0.8 mg, but 8 mg has been drawn up in error. By how many milligrams is the drawn-up dose too large? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: Excess = 8 - 0.8 = 7.2 mg. Line up the decimal points: 8.0 - 0.8 = 7.2.

whyNot.0: The point has been moved one place too far left.
whyNot.1: The point has been moved one place too far right.
whyNot.2: Added the two doses; the excess is the difference.

B.q: A 200 mL bottle contains 1.6 g of a medicine mixed evenly through the liquid. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL?
B.why: 1.6 g = 1600 mg. 1600 mg ÷ 200 mL = 8 mg in each 1 mL. Sense check: 8 mg x 200 mL = 1600 mg.

whyNot.0: 1.6 ÷ 200 gives 0.008 g; the grams were not converted to milligrams.
whyNot.3: Tenfold error the other way: 1600 mg ÷ 200 mL is 8 mg per mL.

C.q: A person takes 2 tablets a day for 10 days. Each tablet contains 0.075 mg. How many milligrams do they take in total? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: Tablets = 2 x 10 = 20. 0.075 x 20 = 1.5 mg. Sense check: 0.075 is just under a tenth, and 20 tenths would be 2 mg.

whyNot.1: The x10 for the days was missed or the point moved the wrong way.
whyNot.3: Counted 1 tablet a day; the person takes 2 a day for 10 days (20 tablets).

C.q: A syringe holds 0.4 mL of a solution that contains 2.5 mg in each 1 mL. How many milligrams are in the syringe?
C.why: Amount = 2.5 mg per mL x 0.4 mL = 1 mg. Sense check: less than half a millilitre holds less than half of 2.5 mg.

whyNot.1: Tenfold error the other way: 2.5 x 0.4 = 1.
whyNot.3: Divided 2.5 by 0.4; the amount is strength x volume.

C.q: A pack holds 1000 sachets, each containing 0.025 g of powder. How many grams of powder are in the whole pack?
C.why: 0.025 x 1000: move the point three places right = 25 g.

whyNot.0: The point moved two places, not three.
whyNot.2: The point moved four places; x1000 moves it three.
whyNot.3: The point moved one place; x1000 moves it three places right.

reteach.title: The point stays still; the digits move
reteach.question: If you multiply 0.06 by 100, which way do the digits slide and how far?

blocks.body: Imagine the decimal point fixed on the page. Multiplying by 10 slides every digit one column to the left, so each is worth ten times more; dividing slides them right. 0.06 x 100 slides the 6 two columns left, from hundredths to units: 6. Fill any empty columns with zeros and always keep a zero in the units column for values below 1.

blocks.text: If an answer suddenly needs a tablet count of 10 or an oral volume of 50 mL, suspect a decimal slip before you type it.

explain.body: To the right of the point the columns are tenths, hundredths and thousandths. In 0.375, the 3 is 0.3, the 7 is 0.07 and the 5 is 0.005.

test.q: In a dose of 0.375 mg, what value does the digit 7 represent?
test.why: The 7 is the second digit after the point: hundredths, worth 0.07 mg.

whyNot.0: That would be the tenths column; the 7 is in the hundredths column.
whyNot.1: That would be the thousandths column, where the 5 sits.
whyNot.2: That would be the units column; this dose is less than 1 mg.

explain.body: Dividing by 100 moves the point two places left. 12.5 ÷ 100 = 0.125. Add a leading zero so the answer starts 0.

test.q: A total of 12.5 mg is divided by 100. What is the result?
test.why: ÷100 moves the point two places left: 12.5 becomes 0.125 mg.

whyNot.0: Moved the point one place; ÷100 moves it two.
whyNot.1: Moved the point three places; ÷100 moves it two.

explain.body: Pearson wants significant digits only: no trailing zeros, a leading zero below 1, the standard abbreviation (mL, mg) and no extra words or an "s".

test.q: A calculation gives 3.50 mL and the question asks you to use the correct unit. What should you type?
test.why: Significant digits only, with the standard abbreviation: 3.5 mL.

whyNot.0: Trailing zeros are not significant and are not the accepted form.
whyNot.2: Pearson lists "mls" as an incorrect unit.
whyNot.3: Pearson asks for the standard abbreviation, not the unit in full.

explain.body: Before calculating, round the numbers and predict the size of the answer. A result ten times bigger or smaller than your estimate means a point has moved.

items.label: estimate: 0.5 mg per mL x 5 mL

test.q: A solution contains 0.5 mg in each 1 mL. A colleague says 5 mL contains 25 mg. How many milligrams do 5 mL actually contain? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
test.why: 0.5 mg x 5 = 2.5 mg. Sense check: half a milligram per mL, five mL, two and a half milligrams.

whyNot.0: This is the colleague's tenfold error.
whyNot.1: Tenfold error the other way: 0.5 x 5 = 2.5.
whyNot.2: Divided 5 by 0.5; the amount is strength x volume.
